task.goal: Help residents compare two municipal waste-sorting instructions that use different terms.
hard_constraints: One page of printed guidance and one volunteer translator; no claim of legal authority.
Do not merge conflicting rules silently; preserve source dates and exceptions.
Test whether readers sort unfamiliar items correctly and know when to ask.
task.available_resources: Two official leaflets and a list of common questions.
task.expected_result: A clear comparison aid and update rule.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Parallel terminology crosswalk
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Create a one-page table that lets residents compare the two vocabularies without treating them as interchangeable. Each row pairs a term from leaflet A with its closest counterpart in leaflet B, gives a plain-language meaning, and records whether their coverage matches, overlaps, or conflicts. Where there is no counterpart, say so. Keep exceptions alongside the relevant term rather than in distant footnotes. The mechanism is explicit comparison: readers can see when different words describe the same instruction and when similar words conceal different rules.

The volunteer translator checks both original terms and plain-language explanations, using the common-question list to prioritize confusing distinctions. Include each leaflet’s title, issuing body, date, and applicable area if stated; label missing dates as unknown. Mark the aid as an unofficial comparison. Conflicting or unclear entries say “check before sorting,” with any clarification route actually supplied by the leaflets.

This requires enough space to retain consequential exceptions in readable type. It assumes most confusion concerns terminology; translation alone cannot resolve policy differences. Update rule: when either leaflet changes, recheck every paired entry and exception, replace the printed page, and record the new source dates. Do not describe either source as superseded without evidence.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the draft with the two leaflets alone using a few residents and six unfamiliar items whose treatment is supported by the sources. Include an exception and an unresolved conflict. Ask for the destination, the supporting instruction, and whether clarification is needed. Prewrite answers from the leaflets; score unresolved cases as requiring a question, not a guessed bin. Reject or revise the crosswalk if it increases confident errors, hides a conflict, or fails to improve interpretation of differently named categories. This small check can expose problems but cannot establish population-wide effectiveness.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A source-separated decision path
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Build a one-page decision tree that starts with the situation governing the instruction, then guides residents through the distinctions actually stated in the leaflets. If the sources specify different areas, services, or collection arrangements, make that the first branch. If applicability cannot be established, route the reader to “ask which instruction applies.” Within each source’s branch, ask short questions about relevant item characteristics, preparation, or exceptions. Retain that leaflet’s category names at the endpoints.

The mechanism is procedural: readers answer observable questions instead of first translating category labels. The volunteer translator converts source wording into short questions and checks that every endpoint and exception remains traceable to the corresponding leaflet. Use the common questions to choose the most useful paths. Print the source titles and dates, explain that the page is unofficial, and visibly flag conflicting instructions rather than selecting a winner.

This works only if the rules can be expressed as a small number of reliable questions. If the tree becomes cramped or depends on facts residents cannot observe, it is unsuitable. Update rule: a changed leaflet triggers a review of the applicability branch and every affected question, endpoint, and exception; replace the page with its revised source dates.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the tree with a simple two-column summary of the same instructions. Ask a few residents to sort unfamiliar items covering ordinary paths, an exception, and uncertain applicability. Record their answers and the branches they followed. Check both correct sorting under the applicable source and stopping to ask when the source cannot be selected. The mechanism is undermined if readers repeatedly choose the wrong first branch, cannot answer a question, or reach a confident endpoint for an unresolved case. Inspect the paths before attributing mistakes to translation.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Contrast pairs that teach rule boundaries
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use one printed page to teach residents how small item differences change the instruction. Select a few common questions and turn them into paired examples: two items or conditions differing in one feature that the leaflets explicitly treat differently. Beside each pair, state the deciding feature and show leaflet A’s and leaflet B’s instructions separately. Use text examples drawn from the supplied materials; do not invent disposal rules. Finish with a short transfer prompt: “Which feature matters here? Does your leaflet cover it? If not, ask.”

The mechanism is learning through contrast. Residents practice identifying the rule boundary, which may help them classify unfamiliar items beyond the examples shown. The volunteer translator checks the examples and explains unfamiliar terms while preserving original category labels. Include source titles, dates, relevant exceptions, an unofficial-status statement, and a visible indication wherever the sources disagree. Use only clarification contacts already provided in the materials.

This requires the leaflets to contain a few clear, generalizable distinctions. Its main limit is overgeneralization: examples may suggest broader rules than the sources support. Update rule: when either source changes, revalidate every example and its stated boundary, replace affected pairs, and print the revised dates. If too few valid contrasts exist, use a direct comparison table instead.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Give a few residents either the contrast page with a brief volunteer explanation or an equally brief explanation using a conventional category list. Then present unfamiliar items that share the relevant features but were absent from the examples, including one exception and one case the sources do not resolve. Ask residents to explain the deciding feature and identify when to ask. Revise or reject the approach if it improves recall of examples but fails on unfamiliar items, encourages unsupported analogies, or reduces appropriate requests for clarification. Keep this an exploratory user check, not a claimed effectiveness result.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A teach-back sheet that exposes misunderstandings
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make the volunteer’s correction of residents’ interpretations the main mechanism. Use one printed page containing two clearly separated source panels and a short teach-back exercise. Each panel retains its leaflet’s category terms, explains the distinctions prioritized by the common-question list, and places consequential exceptions beside the relevant instruction. Include source titles, dates or “date unknown,” and stated applicability. Label the page “Unofficial comparison”; display disagreements explicitly without choosing a winner.

During a brief conversation, the volunteer asks the resident to explain what each leaflet would require for an item and why. The volunteer checks that explanation against the originals, identifies any lost condition or mistaken equivalence, and asks the resident to explain the corrected distinction using another example. Finish by having the resident explain when they would ask for help: uncertain applicability, conflicting instructions, or an item the sources do not cover. Use only clarification routes actually provided in the materials; otherwise acknowledge that no route is supplied.

What changes the outcome is feedback on the resident’s interpretation before it becomes a sorting habit. This could reveal misunderstandings that a readable translation alone leaves hidden. It requires the volunteer to understand both texts and residents to have time for a short exchange. It cannot settle policy ambiguity, and benefit may depend on continued volunteer availability. Keep the originals available for checking; if essential exceptions cannot fit legibly, narrow the page’s stated coverage.

Update rule: whenever either leaflet changes, recheck both panels and the exercise prompts, replace the page, and show the revised source dates. Do not infer that the newer leaflet overrides the other.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Give a few residents the same sheet, with either a brief read-through or an equally timed teach-back conversation. Then independently ask them to sort unfamiliar, source-supported items and identify when to ask, including an exception and an unresolved case. Establish expected answers from the originals beforehand. Revise or reject the mechanism if feedback fails to reduce interpretation errors, creates confident guesses about unresolved cases, or requires explanations the volunteer cannot reliably provide. This checks feasibility and exposes failures; it does not establish general effectiveness.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Preempt misleading shortcuts
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Create a one-page comparison aid organized around tempting but unsupported shortcuts, such as assuming that similar category names cover the same items or that a newer date automatically makes the other leaflet irrelevant. The mechanism is preventive error correction: explain why a shortcut can fail before residents use it, and replace it with a specific checking habit. Unlike teaching category definitions, this targets how residents decide whether an apparent match is trustworthy.

The volunteer translator uses the common questions to identify up to three plausible shortcuts, retaining only those for which the supplied leaflets demonstrate a consequential problem. Each entry contains the tempting assumption, brief supporting excerpts from both leaflets, a plain-language explanation of the difference, and the condition or exception residents must check. Present the two sources separately throughout. Close with explicit reasons to ask: uncertain applicability, conflicting instructions, or missing coverage. Include any clarification route supplied by the materials; acknowledge if none is supplied.

Print source titles, dates or “date unknown,” stated applicability, and “Unofficial comparison; no legal authority.” Preserve relevant exceptions beside each entry. If space is insufficient, narrow and label the page’s coverage. This requires only the leaflets, question list, one page, and the translator. It assumes misleading shortcuts contribute to confusion; the question list may not establish that. If the sources provide no defensible examples, this approach is unsuitable.

Update rule: when either leaflet changes, recheck every quoted passage, correction, and exception, replace the page, and display the revised source dates. Never infer precedence from date alone.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the page with an equally brief, source-separated summary. Ask a few residents to sort unfamiliar items supported by the leaflets, including an exception, and assess an unresolved case. Establish expected answers from the originals beforehand. Record correct destinations, confident errors, and appropriate requests for clarification. Reject or revise the approach if residents repeat the warned-against shortcuts, become indiscriminately hesitant on clear cases, or perform no better than the summary. This is a small feasibility check, not evidence of general effectiveness.

EXPAND.title: Teach-back to expose and repair translation misunderstandings
EXPAND.proposal:
Use the volunteer as a feedback loop: residents explain an instruction in their own words before applying it, allowing the volunteer to detect a mistaken interpretation that a readable comparison sheet might leave hidden.

Prepare one printed page with short, separately attributed excerpts from both leaflets addressing the most consequential common questions. Preserve original category terms, source titles and dates, and relevant exceptions; mark missing dates as unknown. Identify disagreements explicitly and label the page an unofficial aid. Select only as much material as fits legibly, with an explicit instruction to consult the leaflets for omitted topics.

During a brief encounter, the resident chooses a confusing instruction and explains what it would mean for an item. The volunteer asks which wording supports that interpretation, checks it against each applicable leaflet, and repairs any translation error. The resident then restates the corrected meaning and applies it to a different item. This exchange checks understanding rather than merely asking whether the explanation was clear.

The volunteer may explain language but must not decide unresolved policy conflicts. If applicability, an exception, or an instruction remains unclear, identify the exact unresolved question and use any clarification route printed in the sources. Otherwise leave it explicitly unresolved.

This requires residents willing to participate and enough volunteer time for individual exchanges. It assumes the volunteer can interpret both leaflets reliably; teach-back cannot independently validate the volunteer’s own translation. When either leaflet changes, recheck the page’s excerpts, exceptions, and explanations, replace the page, and show the revised source dates.
EXPAND.experiment: The volunteer owns a first trial with six residents, alternating between teach-back and an equally timed explanation using the prior parallel crosswalk. Both conditions use the same source coverage. Then ask residents to classify three unfamiliar items, including an exception and an unresolved case, and explain when they would ask. Prepare source-supported scoring beforehand. Record correct sorting, appropriate questions, confident errors, and minutes per resident. Stop and repair immediately if an explanation contradicts a source. Retain teach-back only if it exposes or reduces misunderstanding without an impractical increase in volunteer time; otherwise the crosswalk is the simpler option. This trial can reveal failures, not establish general effectiveness.

EXPAND.title: Calibrate the decision to sort or ask
EXPAND.proposal:
Make the main intervention practice in deciding whether the available evidence is sufficient to act. A reader can understand both vocabularies yet still guess when neither leaflet supports a conclusion, or ask unnecessarily when the instruction is clear.

Prepare one unofficial printed page containing separately attributed source instructions for selected common questions and three brief practice cases. Include both leaflet titles and dates, relevant exceptions, and visible disagreements; identify unknown dates. Keep the original category terms beside translated explanations. The volunteer checks every practice answer against the leaflets before use.

For each practice case, the resident chooses either a source-supported destination or “ask,” then states the missing or sufficient evidence. Use a close pair on opposite sides of the action boundary: one case with explicit coverage and established applicability, and a minimally changed case whose treatment or applicability the sources leave unresolved. Add one unfamiliar case requiring the same judgment. If the supplied materials cannot support a defensible close pair, do not use this route.

The volunteer gives immediate feedback on both unnecessary hesitation and unsupported confidence. The working rule is to sort when the applicable source explicitly supports the item and its conditions; otherwise identify the uncertainty before seeking clarification. Conflicting sources remain separate, and the volunteer does not adjudicate them. Use only clarification contacts actually supplied; absent a contact, record the question as unresolved.

The mechanism is feedback on the handoff threshold, rather than learning category equivalents or item contrasts. Its limit is that conservative practice may increase questions. Replace the page whenever a source changes, revalidate the practice boundary and exceptions, and print the new source dates.
EXPAND.experiment: The volunteer owns a six-resident pilot comparing this practice with the prior source-separated decision path, allowing the same preparation coverage and recording actual interaction time. After instruction, present a new close pair straddling the act-versus-ask boundary and one unfamiliar case. Score destination accuracy, appropriate handoff, unnecessary handoff, and confident unsupported sorting against answers established from the leaflets. Stop immediately if feedback suppresses a warranted question or treats a conflict as settled. Revise or abandon the route if it adds volunteer time or unnecessary referrals without improving justified action and handoff choices. Report individual errors rather than claiming effectiveness from this small check.

EXPAND.title: Crosswalk with a rule for entries that cannot fit safely
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the parallel terminology crosswalk, the strongest direct comparison route. Keep paired original terms, plain-language explanations, match/overlap/conflict labels, separately attributed instructions, and exceptions beside their terms. Add an operational rule for incomplete entries: the volunteer must not print a usable sorting destination for a row unless both sources’ relevant conditions and exceptions fit legibly. Instead, print the terms and “consult the full instruction before sorting,” identifying the relevant section in each leaflet. This prevents an abbreviated comparison from appearing sufficient when its omitted conditions could change the answer.

The volunteer owns preparation using only the two leaflets and common questions. Prioritize consequential, frequently asked distinctions. Print source titles, issuing bodies, dates and stated applicability; mark missing information unknown. Label the single page an unofficial comparison. Preserve disagreements explicitly and use only clarification routes supplied in the materials. Residents may act only when the applicable source and the complete printed instruction support the item; unresolved coverage or conflict requires a question. If the volunteer is unavailable or an exchange is interrupted, the printed restriction remains in force; an unanswered question is not clearance to sort.

This assumes enough complete comparisons fit on one legible page to be useful. Compared with the original crosswalk, the change sacrifices some immediate answers and may increase leaflet consultation, but reduces the risk of acting on compressed rules. If too few entries qualify, retain a short terminology comparison with source pointers rather than shrink text or omit exceptions. When either leaflet changes, the volunteer rechecks all pairings, conditions and exceptions, replaces the page, and records the new source dates; pending review, affected entries revert to source consultation.
EXPAND.experiment: The volunteer first audits every actionable row against both leaflets; any omitted condition that could change sorting stops distribution until repaired. Then run a small exploratory check with six residents, alternating the revised page and an equally legible original-style crosswalk with the same topic coverage. Use unfamiliar items supported by the supplied materials, including a clear actionable case, a closely related case requiring consultation because of a consequential condition, and an unresolved conflict. Establish source-supported answers beforehand. Record correct destinations, warranted questions, unnecessary questions, confident errors, and time spent consulting leaflets or the volunteer. Stop and repair if an incomplete row produces a confident destination. Keep the added restriction only if it prevents consequential misunderstanding at an acceptable consultation burden; otherwise reduce coverage to fully printable entries. This trial can expose failures, not establish superiority.

EXPAND.title: Decision path with an explicit exit for unanswerable questions
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the source-separated decision path, a competitive route because it helps readers apply rules without first mastering category vocabulary. Preserve the applicability-first branch, separate source paths, original category names, visible conflicts and relevant exceptions. Change the everyday procedure by giving every decision question an explicit “cannot tell” exit. That exit identifies the missing fact and directs the reader to the corresponding source passage or an available clarification route; it never defaults to a bin.

The volunteer builds the one-page unofficial aid from the two leaflets, prioritizing the common questions. For each question, the volunteer checks whether the resident can establish its answer from the item or the supplied instructions. If not, replace that branch with a consultation endpoint rather than asking residents to infer an unavailable fact. Print source titles, dates and stated applicability, marking unknown information. Conflicts remain separately attributed. The volunteer may explain wording but cannot settle policy disagreements.

The decision boundary is concrete: follow a branch only when its required fact is established. On an interrupted explanation, the resident returns to the last established fact and treats the next unanswered question as unresolved. Until clarification is actually obtained, responsibility remains with the resident to avoid treating that case as resolved; the volunteer does not promise a referral outcome. If no clarification route is supplied, identify the unanswered question and leave it unresolved without inventing a disposal instruction.

This requires a short enough tree to remain legible and enough source detail to support observable questions. Compared with the original tree, explicit exits may increase consultation but reduce forced guesses. If the exits dominate or the tree becomes crowded, fall back to separate source excerpts with clearly marked unresolved questions. Any source change triggers volunteer review of applicability, questions, endpoints and exceptions, replacement of the page, and revised source dates.
EXPAND.experiment: The volunteer audits each branch for a supported answer and a usable uncertainty exit before a six-resident exploratory trial. Compare the revised tree with the original-style tree over identical source coverage. Include a source-supported close pair: one case whose deciding fact can be established and one whose deciding fact cannot, plus another unfamiliar item and an exception. If the materials cannot support such cases, do not claim to have tested the exit mechanism. Ask for destinations, the path taken, and when clarification is required. Record correct sorting, appropriate and unnecessary questions, confident errors, completion time and volunteer assistance. Briefly interrupt one practice explanation to inspect whether the reader resumes from an established fact. Stop and repair any branch that turns uncertainty into a confident destination. Retain the change only if its reduction in unsupported decisions justifies the extra stops; otherwise simplify the tree or use the stated excerpt fallback.
